summary: Describes the route optimization problem in NEMO Basic Support. All traffic to and from nodes in a mobile network goes through a tunnel between the mobile router and the home agent when away, which adds delay and can cause congestion. This memo states the problem. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Even if your neighbor is next door, mail takes a trip through your faraway home post office and back. This note explains why that is wasteful.

questions: what is the nemo route optimization problem
subtitle: Why mobile networks need faster routes to avoid bottlenecks

tldr.problem: Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support forces all traffic from a mobile network through a tunnel to the home agent, creating inefficient routes, bottlenecks, and worse problems in nested mobile networks.
tldr.mechanism: The document catalogs the specific problems caused by mandatory home agent tunneling: longer delays, packet overhead, processing load, fragmentation risk, bottleneck congestion, amplified problems with nested networks, and impossible stalemate situations.
tldr.outcome: This informational document establishes the need for route optimization in NEMO, showing that optimization is more critical for NEMO than it was for Mobile IPv6 alone.

facts.label: Nesting levels
facts.value: Multiple allowed, each adds header and delay

today: RFC 4888 is informational and remains the standard problem statement for NEMO route optimization. It motivated the work that produced solutions such as RFC 5845, which defined a Mobile Router Position mechanism for nested NEMO optimization. The issues it describes remain active research and deployment challenges for mobile network implementations.

sections.title: NEMO Basic Support and Its Limitations
sections.content:
Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support is a protocol that allows an entire mobile network (such as a network aboard a train or airplane) to maintain connectivity when moving. All communications to and from nodes in the mobile network go through a bi-directional tunnel between the Mobile Router (the network's gateway) and its Home Agent (a server at the home network).

While this tunnel ensures connectivity, it creates sub-optimal routes. Packets travel from a mobile network node to the home agent, then to their final destination—even when a direct path exists. This approach works but comes with significant performance penalties that worsen when mobile networks nest inside other mobile networks.
sections.eli5: When a network moves to a new place, it keeps a tunnel to home so it stays connected. But sending mail through home is slow even if the neighbor is right next door.

sections.title: The Sub-Optimality of NEMO Basic Routing
sections.content:
The mandatory use of home agent tunneling creates multiple inefficiencies. Longer routes increase packet delay, which harms real-time applications like multimedia and degrades TCP performance by increasing round-trip time. The tunnel also creates additional infrastructure load by forcing packets to traverse longer network paths.

Encapsulation overhead adds an extra IPv6 header (40 bytes) to each packet. For voice applications transmitting at 8 kbps with 20 millisecond samples, this encapsulation header is twice the payload size, halving bandwidth efficiency. Processing delay at encapsulation and decapsulation points includes encryption, topological verification, MTU computation, fragmentation, and reassembly.

Packet fragmentation becomes more likely due to the larger packets, further increasing delays. Finally, the longer routing path means higher probability of encountering link failures, reducing reliability compared to a direct route.
sections.eli5: Going through home makes everything slower, fatter, and more likely to break. Even a small voice call becomes half junk data instead of real voice.

sections.title: Bottlenecks and Cascading Failures in Nested Networks
sections.content:
All traffic passing through the home agent can create a bottleneck at the home network itself. The home agent or home link may not have capacity for the aggregated traffic from all mobile network nodes. When congestion occurs, packets are delayed or lost, degrading performance. Additionally, security check, packet interception, and tunneling operations on the home agent may not be as optimized as simple forwarding, further limiting capacity.

With the home link as a single point of failure, any outage blocks all communication. Binding Update signaling messages may be delayed or lost due to congestion, preventing the establishment of tunnels and disrupting all traffic.

Nested mobile networks (mobile routers attaching to other mobile routers) amplify these problems exponentially. A packet from a deeply nested node must traverse multiple MRHA tunnels, adding multiple IPv6 headers at each level. Each level adds processing delay and fragmentation risk. The home link of each upstream mobile router becomes a single point of failure for all downstream traffic.
sections.eli5: Home becomes a traffic jam. Each level of nesting doubles the junk headers and adds another weak link where everything can fail.

sections.title: Additional Problems: Security Policy and Stalemate Situations
sections.content:
Security administrators may forbid visiting mobile nodes (nodes from other networks) from tunneling traffic back to the home network, fearing attacks. This blocks legitimate nested NEMO deployments where mobile routers depend on each other without prior security associations. Route optimization could solve this by allowing direct forwarding without tunneling.

Within a nested mobile network, two mobile network nodes on different links under the same root router cannot communicate directly—their traffic must go out to the home agent and back. This is wasteful and can cause instability. If the root router loses Internet connectivity, nodes cannot communicate even though their local path is unaffected.

A stalemate situation occurs when a parent mobile router visits one of its child mobile routers. The child cannot find its home agent (it is nested behind the parent) and thus cannot establish its tunnel to receive the parent's traffic. The parent cannot bind to its own home agent because it is not on the Internet. Communications deadlock until the situation is manually resolved or the networks separate.
sections.eli5: Home office bans outside visitors from using its mail system. Kids can't talk to each other without going through home. Parents visiting children create a deadlock where nobody can bind.

sections.title: The Case for Route Optimization
sections.content:
These problems collectively demonstrate that Route Optimization for NEMO is not merely an enhancement—it is essential for viable deployments, especially with nested networks. Route optimization can bypass the home agent entirely in some cases, avoiding bottlenecks, reducing latency, and decreasing infrastructure load. It can enable deployments currently blocked by security policy and prevent stalemate situations.

The problem is more acute for NEMO than for Mobile IPv6 alone, because the amplification effect of nesting makes basic support increasingly unusable. Where Mobile IPv6 route optimization was a performance improvement, NEMO route optimization is often a requirement for connectivity. This document establishes the problem space and motivation for standardizing route optimization solutions.
sections.eli5: Skipping home is not a nice-to-have—it is the only way many mobile networks can work at all, especially when they are nested or complex.
